impeccable

im-PEK-uh-bul -- stress on the second syllable, PEK. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Impeccable is so perfect that no fault can be found anywhere.

His impeccable manners impressed even the host's grandmother, who was famously hard to please.

Example

A pastry chef sends out forty identical tarts, each one impeccable: every crust the same shade of gold, every fruit slice at the same angle, not one drip on any of the forty plates.

Impeccable means flawless, spotless, faultless -- the very top grade of 'no mistakes.' It does not mean 'very good'; it means 'nothing anywhere is wrong.'

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

flawless: Flawless points at the thing itself: a flawless diamond, a flawless complexion -- no defect exists in the object. Impeccable is praise for how something is done -- manners, timing, taste -- measured against the strictest judge and found beyond criticism. A stone is flawless; conduct is impeccable.

polished: Polished praises the smoothness that rehearsal gives -- confident, practiced, pleasant to watch. But polished work can still leave a judge something to correct. Impeccable makes the stronger claim: nothing anywhere is wrong, so there is nothing left to fix.

pristine: Pristine means in its original, untouched condition -- fresh snow, a book never opened. The emphasis is on being unused and unmarked, not on passing inspection. Impeccable is earned the opposite way: through performance, by doing something so well that no fault can be found in it.

exemplary: Exemplary praises work as a model for others to copy -- so good it deserves imitation. Exemplary work can still contain a small slip and remain a fine example. Impeccable is stricter and narrower: not a model to follow, but a performance in which no fault exists at all.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

flawed: containing faults or errors

shoddy: carelessly made or carelessly done

Where it sits · how high the standard of perfection — faultless → impeccable → immaculate

faultless vs. impeccable: Faultless stops at the plain fact that no mistakes were made, while impeccable climbs higher -- a standard so demanding that even the harshest critic could not find one thing left to fix.

immaculate vs. impeccable: Immaculate goes even further than impeccable, from 'no faults' to 'no trace': impeccable work survives the strictest inspection, while an immaculate result looks untouched -- not a smudge, a speck, or a fingerprint anywhere on it.

Build the Word

The pieces

prefix — im-

prefix — im-: not (the form in- takes before p) (Latin in-)

root — peccable

root — peccable: capable of sinning or erring (Latin peccare 'to sin, to make a mistake')

Put it together

Put it together: Impeccable is this unit's prefix in its im- form (in- shifts to im- before p) on Latin peccare ('to sin'), so the literal reading is 'not capable of sinning' -- incapable of a single fault. The honest caveat: 'peccable' is technically an English word but so rare that almost no one has seen it, which makes this split likely rather than confirmed. The root does surface in a word real people use: peccadillo, a small sin.

Use the root in a new word: peccadillo

Use the root in a new word: peccadillo: In her diary she kept a running list of the week's peccadilloes.

Root Check

Word Choice

Impeccable is praise without reservation: impeccable timing, impeccable manners, an impeccable record, impeccable taste. Because it literally means 'incapable of sin,' it is an absolute -- something either is impeccable or it is not, and 'fairly impeccable' does not work.
